title: NPCI's MDR-Funded Scheme Pays Banks to Put UPI QR Codes in Small-Town Shops
excerpt: The UPI Vyapaar Saksham Scheme recycles 5% of future MDR collections into Rs 300-per-QR and Rs 750-per-soundbox incentives for banks onboarding small merchants in Tier III-VI cities, the Northeast, J&K and Ladakh.
body:
• NPCI has launched the UPI Vyapaar Saksham Scheme, paying acquiring banks Rs 300 per physical QR code and Rs 750 per soundbox deployed at eligible new small merchants.
  • The scheme is funded from UPI merchant discount rate (MDR) collections: every ecosystem participant contributes 5% of its MDR share, split 30% for onboarding, 50% for transaction growth and 20% for incremental growth in targeted geographies.
  • It targets merchants with annual turnover up to Rs 40 lakh in Tier III to Tier VI cities, the Northeast, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, and runs for three years from the implementation of UPI MDR, which is yet to be notified.
  • For diaspora readers: the change is on the merchant side only. UPI payments up to Rs 2,000 and person-to-person transfers stay outside the MDR framework, and consumers are not charged.

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) has introduced the UPI Vyapaar Saksham Scheme, a three-year programme that will pay banks to put UPI QR codes and soundboxes into the hands of small merchants in smaller towns and underserved regions. Announced in a circular dated November 11, the scheme is funded not by a government allocation but from the merchant discount rate (MDR) that banks and payment companies will earn once UPI MDR takes effect.

Under the scheme, NPCI defines a small merchant as a business with annual turnover of up to Rs 40 lakh in the preceding financial year. The focus is on merchants in Tier III to Tier VI cities, the northeastern states, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. Small merchants covered under notified central government schemes, including PM SVANidhi and PM Vishwakarma, are also eligible, according to Inc42's report on the circular.

How the MDR fund works

MDR is the fee a merchant's bank and other payment participants earn for processing a digital payment. NPCI's scheme pools a slice of that income: each issuing bank, acquiring bank, payer payment service provider (PSP) and UPI app provider participating in UPI will contribute 5% of its MDR share to the fund. The contribution excludes MDR earned from categories that are not eligible for the scheme.

"The first, accounting for 30% of the fund, pays acquiring banks Rs 300 for every physical QR code and Rs 750 for every soundbox deployed at an eligible new small merchant."

The fund is divided into three components. The first, accounting for 30% of the fund, pays acquiring banks Rs 300 for every physical QR code and Rs 750 for every soundbox deployed at an eligible new small merchant. To qualify, a merchant must record at least 25 eligible transactions in any two months of a quarter, with a minimum transaction value of Rs 5,000 per month. Eligible transactions are successfully settled UPI payments of up to Rs 2,000 at small merchants; reversed, refunded, cancelled or artificially split payments do not count.

The second component, at 50% of the fund, rewards acquiring banks for growing UPI transaction volumes among existing and newly onboarded small merchants. Banks must show at least 5% quarter-on-quarter growth in eligible transaction volumes to qualify, and receive 0.03% of the aggregate value of eligible transactions, with an additional 50% incentive for merchants in the targeted geographies. The remaining 20% goes to incremental growth in those geographies, paying 0.2% of the incremental value of eligible transactions over the previous quarter, on top of the second component.

Targets and administration

NPCI expects the scheme to facilitate 6 lakh to 1 crore new physical QR code deployments and 5 lakh to 10 lakh new soundbox installations annually, and to drive 30% to 50% annual growth in transaction volumes among existing small merchants. NPCI will administer the fund, validate incentive claims and oversee settlements. Acquiring banks will submit claims quarterly, and NPCI is required to process incentive payments within 30 days of claim submission, subject to validation. Banks must also report merchant locations, unique merchant identifiers and details of deployed QR codes and soundboxes for transaction-level monitoring.

Why MDR is returning

The scheme arrives as the Centre prepares to reintroduce MDR on select high-value UPI transactions after nearly six years of a zero-MDR regime. In September 2026, the government notified amendments to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, paving the way for MDR on select merchant transactions. Under the framework NPCI subsequently introduced, person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000 attract an MDR of 0.4%, capped at Rs 300 for transactions of Rs 75,000 and above. The full framework is on NPCI's published MDR details as summarised in coverage of its Supreme Court affidavit.

Transactions of up to Rs 2,000 and peer-to-peer payments stay outside the MDR framework, and small merchants receiving up to Rs 1 lakh per month through UPI QR codes under the person-to-person-merchant category were also exempted. The rollout has been pushed back once already: the imposition was deferred beyond Diwali, and NPCI has not yet announced an implementation date. The Vyapaar Saksham Scheme runs for three years from that implementation, whenever it is notified.

What it means for merchants and customers

For a small merchant in a Tier IV town, the practical effect is that their bank now gets paid to onboard them and to keep their UPI volumes growing, rather than digital acceptance being concentrated among larger merchants in urban markets. For customers, including visiting NRIs paying by UPI on trips home, nothing changes at the till: the MDR is earned and shared among banks and payment companies, not charged to the person paying, and payments up to Rs 2,000 remain outside the framework entirely.

The next milestone is the MDR implementation date itself. Until NPCI notifies it, the fund the scheme draws on does not exist yet — the circular sets the machinery in place ahead of the revenue stream it will recycle.
